opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's one I think about a lot. Right now, most people interact with these systems through what is essentially a chat box. And chat is wonderful, it's flexible, it's familiar, but it's also a little bit like if the only way we'd ever interacted with computers was the command line. It's powerful, but it hides an enormous amount.

So what I'd love to see over the next few years is a real flowering of experimentation, a lot of weird, playful, ambitious attempts at new kinds of interfaces. In particular, I'm excited about interfaces that take advantage of what we're learning from interpretability. We're starting to understand that these models have internal representations, of things like the topic of a conversation, or even of the user they think they're talking to. And it seems natural to ask: why not show some of that to people? Imagine a dashboard where you could see what the model seems to believe about you, and maybe even adjust it. That could be useful for transparency, and it raises really interesting design questions about control and trust.

More broadly, I'd like experimentation to be something lots of people can do, not just a handful of big labs. Some of the most interesting ideas in visualization and interface design historically came from individuals and small groups just trying things. So I hope we get tools, open models, and a culture that make it easy for designers, artists, and researchers to prototype quickly and share what they find, including the failures.

And finally, I'd like us to be a little more rigorous about evaluating these interfaces. Not in a way that kills creativity, but in a way where we actually learn what helps people understand and work with these systems, and what just looks cool. If we can combine that sense of play with real attention to human needs, I think the next three years could be a remarkably fertile time.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. The thing I keep coming back to is that we're at this strange moment where the underlying models have gotten incredibly capable, and yet the way most people interact with them is a text box. A chat window. And I think history tells us that the interface is not an afterthought. If you look at the personal computer, the ideas were there in the sixties, but it was the graphical interface, the mouse, direct manipulation, that actually let ordinary people use the thing. I suspect we're in a similar pre-GUI era for AI.

So over the next three years, what I'd love to see is a lot more willingness to be weird. Right now there's a strong gravitational pull toward one paradigm, the conversational assistant, partly because it works reasonably well and partly because it's the easiest thing to ship. But conversation is actually a pretty low-bandwidth channel. When I'm working with data, or a piece of writing, or a design, I don't want to describe what I want in sentences. I want to point, to drag, to see a space of possibilities laid out and pick from it. I'd like to see interfaces that treat the model less as an oracle you query and more as a kind of material you shape.

The second thing, and this comes out of the interpretability work I've been involved with, is that I think the interface and the internals of these systems are going to become more connected than people expect. If you can actually read something about what the model is representing, what it's attending to, what it's uncertain about, then that's not just a research curiosity. That's raw material for an interface. Imagine a writing tool that doesn't just suggest text but shows you, in some visual form, where the model is confident and where it's guessing. That changes the relationship. You stop treating it as an authority and start treating it as a collaborator with visible limitations.

And the third piece is honestly about who gets to do the experimenting. A lot of the most interesting interface ideas in computing history came from people who were a little outside the main institutions, artists, hobbyists, people tinkering. The cost of building a prototype with these models has dropped enormously, which is wonderful. I'd want to see that energy supported rather than funneled into a few product templates. Give people the primitives, let them build strange things, and expect most of them to fail. That's how you find the mouse.

So if I'm being optimistic, three years from now I'd hope the chat box looks a bit like the command line looks today. Still there, still useful for certain people, but clearly one option among many, and no longer the thing we mistake for the whole idea.

astra-6.text:
I’d love to see a much wider range of experiments in how we interact with these systems. Chat is useful, but it’s only one possibility. What would it look like to have an interface where you could see several alternatives at once, manipulate them directly, or get a clearer sense of what happens when you change your instructions?

And I’d like those experiments to help people ask better questions about the system. Where does it work well? Where does it break down? When should you check its work? You don’t necessarily need to expose all the machinery to help someone build a useful understanding of it.

So over the next three years, I’d hope we move beyond making it easy to get an answer and toward making it easy to explore, question, and revise an answer. That seems like a really rich space for design.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d love to see us broaden what we think an AI interface can be. Right now, so much of the experience is a chat box. That’s a useful starting point, but I hope we don’t mistake it for the final answer.

For example, how do you let someone explore several possibilities at once, compare them, and steer the system visually? How do you make it easy to see what the system has changed and undo just part of it? Those are interface questions, and they can make an enormous difference in how much control people have.

Over the next three years, I’d like to see lots of experiments with those questions, followed by careful observation of people actually using the results. Are people understanding more? Are they finding ideas they wouldn’t otherwise have found? Can they recognize when the system is wrong? I’d be excited by interfaces that help people develop their own judgment as well as get something done.
